newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Belgium - death of a country forecast.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Belgium - death of a country forecast.

text.p: Belgian author Jacques Neirynck forecasts that Belgium will fall apart early in the next century -- and recent events have done little to demolish his doomsday scenario.

In his novel "The Siege of Brussels", Neirynck has Flemish fascists capturing part of the capital, the federal goverment crumbling and the king abdicating, bringing the Belgian state to an end 177 years after its creation in 1830.

The author, who lives in voluntary exile in Switzerland, told Reuters in an interview that, for him, Belgium was an artificial state, created after the Napoleonic wars as a buffer between squabbling France and Germany.

He said he would not shed a tear over a country where, in his view, many French speakers are oppressed. "It would be excellent to dissolve (Belgium), just like Czechoslavakia and Yugoslavia were dissolved."

A francophone, he left Belgium a quarter of a century ago to flee what he called victimisation in the Dutch-speaking suburbs of Brussels, itself officially a bilingual city but 85 percent French-speaking according city statistics.
NORTH-SOUTH STRIFE TO HIT BRUSSELS

For Neirynck, the language divide and economic strife between Dutch-speaking Flanders in the north -- a hive of profitable hi-tech industry -- and francophone Wallonia in the south -- a post-industrial wasteland -- will come to a head in Brussels..

Erwin Boze, Neirynck's fictitious rightwing leader of Flanders, marches on Brussels with his troops and seizes most of it without effort, but in the Moslem ghetto of Schaerbeek there are street clashes and fears of ethnic cleansing.

The French army flies in to rescue the francophones and head off the conquest of Wallonia and takes up positions at the gates of the city, the self-proclaimed heart of Europe. The European Union stands by helplessly.
Brief negotiations result in a division of spoils, with Boze taking one third of the city, moving into the king's residence and proclaiming Brussels the capital of an independent Flanders.
French speakers retain a third and a so-called Euro District with EU institutions is given separate status in the final third.
Neirynck said: "I left Belgium 25 years ago because I feared things would take a turn for the worse. I haven't been wrong."
FLEMISH MOVES FOR INDEPENDENCE
His scenario is given credibility by recent trends.

In the face of Flemish claims for an end to capital transfers to the impoverished south and a growing drive for independence, francophone politicians have revived the notion of a "re-attachment" to France.

A third of Dutch speakers, totalling almost six million, support the goal of an independent Flanders, further undermining national sentiment in a country already lacking solidarity between its Germanic and Latin cultural groupings.

Among the Flemish, scandals of recent years, mainly involving corruption in politics and industry but reaching new depths of outrage and shock with the discovery of a child sex, murder and kidnapping ring last August, have sapped the belief in a common state.

Much to the disgust of francophone politicians, some of their Dutch-speaking counterparts have openly dared to claim that the scandals are typical of Wallonia, thus deepening the rift between north and south.
EUROPE TOO?

For Neirynck such outbursts point to what lies ahead -- not just in Belgium, but in Europe as a whole. "Belgium's history is a mirror image of Europe's history. My novel warns that (a unified) Europe will fail because of the same conflict."
Perhaps not surprisingly, the book is a success among French speakers, having sold some 20,000 copies. It has won acclaim from French critics.
In Flanders hardly any copies have been sold and there have been no reviews.
